title: Black Oily Specks Rain Down on Moscow After Ukraine's Largest Drone Barrage Hits Refinery
summary: Specks of black oil rained down on Moscow this week after a Ukrainian drone strike hit the Kapotnya oil refinery, marking the largest such attack on the Russian capital since the full-scale invasion began. Columns of thick smoke billowed into the sky, and 17 people were wounded in the Moscow region, according to local governor Andrei Vorobyov. Despite official denials of "oil rain," verified videos showed a dark, oily sheen coating car parks and residents reported black spots on clothes. "We'll now be keeping an eye on whether our hair starts falling out because of petroleum products," one resident said. Russia's defense ministry claimed almost 1,000 drones and four Ukrainian cruise missiles were intercepted across the country in 24 hours. An oil depot in the southern Rostov region was also struck, killing one person. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attack was retaliation for a Russian strike on Kyiv that set ablaze the historic Pechersk Lavra monastery. "We don't want this war and have never wanted it," Zelensky said. "But if Ukraine burns, your Moscow will burn too." In response, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov vowed strikes on Ukraine "on a mass scale." Moscow's four airports were temporarily shut, and over 500 flights were canceled or delayed. The attack underscores Ukraine's growing long-range drone capabilities and its strategy of "bringing the war home" to ordinary Russians. Drone attacks on Moscow, about 500 kilometers from the Ukrainian border, have become more frequent, though air defenses have been bolstered. However, no system can guarantee total protection against massive swarms. The psychological impact is palpable: one Moscow resident described feeling panic for the first time. The war of attrition grinds on, with both sides escalating strikes deep into each other's territory.
why_it_matters: The strike shows that in modern war, civilians far from the front lines can become targets overnight, and drone technology makes it nearly impossible to guarantee anyone's safety, raising hard questions about how wars will be fought in the future.

background_read: Since Russia’s full‑scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine has developed a fleet of long‑range drones to hit military and energy targets hundreds of kilometers inside Russia. Moscow, about 500 km from the Ukrainian border, had been relatively safe in earlier months, but drone strikes have become more frequent.
The Kapotnya oil refinery is one of the largest near Moscow, and such facilities are critical to Russia’s war effort. Attacks on refineries aim to reduce fuel supplies for tanks and aircraft.

The Pechersk Lavra monastery in Kyiv is a UNESCO World Heritage site; a Russian strike there in early 2025 damaged buildings and sparked outrage, leading President Zelensky (Ukraine’s leader since 2019) to promise a response.
Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov (Russia’s top diplomat since 2004) has repeatedly warned that attacks on Russian soil would be met with severe punishment, raising fears of further escalation.

perspectives.description: For Ukraine, hitting deep into Russia is a way to pressure the Russian government and public, showing that the war has real costs at home. It may also force Russia to pull air defenses away from the front lines, weakening its battlefield position.

Refinery strikes can leak toxic chemicals and cause fires near populated areas, as Moscow experienced. Russian officials promise harsh retaliation, meaning the cycle of strikes could escalate and make a negotiated peace even harder to reach.

A war of attrition is not just about destroying equipment; it's also about wearing down morale. Making ordinary Russians feel unsafe challenges the Kremlin's narrative that the war is distant and under control, potentially influencing domestic politics.

This attack illustrates how cheap, swarming drones can overwhelm expensive air defenses. The world is watching to see if drone swarms become a decisive weapon in future conflicts, leading to new military doctrines and possibly arms control talks.
